utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar would like to make a comment while the witness is coming in, and I am pleased to give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was informed last night, that is, the Registry was, about the problems which the interpreters and stenographers had because of the speed at which people were reading things out, that is, Mr. Nice and the witness. I was asked, and I'm asking you, insofar as possible, that the cadence be slowed down, especially because of the fact that the transcripts from yesterday won't be ready for another three or four days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. If that was the Presiding Judge who said that, there would be no effect, but since it is the registrar, perhaps we can hope that there will be some result. All right. Please be careful. I know that it's difficult. I myself, when I get caught up in my own vehements, I make that same mistake. We'll all have to be careful. Last night, the interpreters were exhausted, and we have got to try to preserve them. Otherwise, nothing is going to work. All right. Good morning to them, and good morning to Prosecution and Defence counsel and to the accused. Mr. Nice, I ask that you proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, we had looked yesterday at the evidence in the form of the transcriptions of the interviews and the various passages upon which you've placed particular reliance. Let's now sum things up. So far as the killings were concerned, did the defendant explain that there were lists of people to be killed?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He having at least one list himself?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he, at various times, explain how victims that he had to kill were identified by their Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there examples of killings, to which he admitted, where he made no enquiry at all of why the person was to be killed?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, where he expressed himself ignorant, even after the event, of why the person had been killed, save for the fact that he was told to kill that person?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There was the one example, of course, of the killing in front of the police station of the escaping man, where on the defendant's own account, there was no completed inquiry that could explain any decision to kill?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did the defendant assert, although we haven't referred to the name, did he assert that others were always in charge of him?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The evidence you understand of authority at the camp may, to some degree, differ with that?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's what I desire to point you to by way of the evidence on the killings, and very shortly I would like you to return to the topic of inconsistencies that we started dealing with yesterday. Probably it's easier if I ask you to amplify matters, insofar as you want to, and remind you and the Judges that the categories that you assert reveal inconsistencies are, first, whether he had no option to leave but had to stay and kill. Would you like to just express your position on that a little bit more?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jelisic claimed that he had to commit the murders, had to stay in Brcko, otherwise he would have been killed, and that he tried to save as many people as he could. There are a number of points from the interviews that I believe are inconsistent with that. The first point is, to put it in context, Mr. Jelisic went to Brcko of his own free will. He heard of a deal that was being offered, and he volunteered to go to Brcko. Your Honours, the passages that I'm making reference to were found yesterday. If it assists, I can simply give the page number and interview date where the relevant questions and answers are as I make these points.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if you can just do that very briefly, without taking time, because we've looked at the passages, and indeed that was why we looked at the passages, so that your conclusions could be well founded.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct. That's on the 4th of June, page 5. The second point is during the interview on the 4th of June, he was asked for the first time what he believed would happen if he did not kill a person he was told to kill. He said that if he did not commit the murder, he would have been assaulted or sent to prison, sent to prison for a crime that he had already been sentenced to. When questioned further, he said that he did not actually receive that threat because he did not protest. He believed that he would have received the threat if he would have protested. That's on pages 24 and 25 of the 4th of June. Your Honours, this was his first formal opportunity to tell us why he had committed a murder and what threat he was labouring under. If he really did fear that he would be killed, I believe that he would have used the opportunity to tell us that, rather than telling us that he believed he would have been assaulted or sent back to prison. His claims that he feared death came later in the interviews and, I believe, may have been an afterthought. The next point I would like to make is it appears that he did not question being told to kill people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's a reference for that in the same 4th of June interview?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Later in the same interview, at page 53 on the English transcripts. The next point I would like to make is that he was clearly able to get out of Brcko in the early stages, that is, after the initial murders. There's reference to that at page 25 on the 4th of June, when he said that there were not many roadblocks and he could have gotten out. He was also able to get around the roadblocks and away from Brcko when he had had enough, which was around the 19th or 20th of May, according to Mr. Jelisic, where he said, "I left Brcko because I didn't want to do any dirty jobs anymore." That's on the 1st of July, pages 6, 7, and 8. The next point is he was also able to drive to Belgrade. He took EU -- European Union Monitors to the Hotel Yugoslavia in Belgrade, mentioned the 30th of June, page 8, and to Bijeljina, where he said he took a Catholic priest; 4th of June, page 54 and 55; and also journalists; 30th of June, page 8 of the transcript. The next point I would like to make is that clearly, before leaving Brcko, he disregarded his instructions to kill and did not have specific problems, according to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's on his account, that he disregarded instructions?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is on his account; 4th of June, page 57. He said, "And again the order was to kill him, and I did the same thing, I put him somewhere else."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You needn't read the rest of the quotation, but it's available to the Court.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: He goes on to say, "It could have happened that I could have had problems. There were no specific problems, but I could have had problems. I could have been killed by one of the crazy guys," and he goes on. The next point is that when he returned to Bijeljina after being away for some time, he was apprehended at a roadblock and taken to the Bijeljina SUP. He was apprehended, according to him, for being a deserter, and he claims that he was assaulted. He claims that this was part of a plan to kill him, yet after being beaten, instead of being taken off somewhere and shot, he was taken to the hospital because they had hurt him. On page 27 of the 1st of July, I said, "So I'm just trying to get this straight. After your beating, you were taken for medical treatment at the emergency services; is that right?" He said, "Yes, not the specials but the ordinary police, regular police." Given the threats he claims were made to him, he could not explain why he was given medical treatment instead of being killed. His answers were, "I have no idea. You have to ask them," which was on page 28 of the 1st of July. And later, when it was put to him again, he said, "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, now that's some of the points that you would wish to make on that central issue of his obligation to stay and do what he was doing or his freedom to move?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've already dealt with how there was the one killing in front of the police station, where there was no concluded interrogation that preceded it, and the page references for that are, and correct me if I'm wrong, the 4th of June at pages 34, 38, and 65, and 66, 73, and 80; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: The first page numbers, pages 34 and 38, relate to that particular killing. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other page references show, I think, willingness in participation.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, it may be of lesser importance and therefore appropriate to be dealt with much more summarily. You also made reference to contradictions or inconsistencies about his time after getting away from Brcko, whether he was hiding out in fear for his life and whether he had run out of money?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The page references are all available and can always be included in any argument, but can you just, first of all, in just a sentence, explain what we've already seen in the evidence you say is important here?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Jelisic claims that after getting away from Brcko, he was hiding out in fear for his life. In the account that he gave of places that he went to after leaving Brcko, he mentions a number of hotels that he checked into, and he gave those details. Hotels in the former Yugoslavia require details when you check in, and it appears to me inconsistent that you would check into a number of hotels, leaving personal particulars for police to check. I also mentioned the conversation yesterday that he had with a member of the special police from Belgrade, where he was told the nickname of the person, that he was from the special police and was ordered to kill him, also that he knew all of Mr. Jelisic's movements. Yet when there was an arrest in Petrovac of two people at the same table for what they had done in Brcko, there was no apparent interest shown by the authorities in him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, on the second topic that I mentioned shortly before, whether he ran out of money.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Jelisic claims that he had to come back to Brcko because he ran out of money. He stated earlier that he believed that he had to leave Brcko in May 1992; otherwise, he would have been killed. The 4th of June, page 58. According to him, he had been forced to commit murders and threatened with death if he did not comply. Clearly, he had not complied, not just once but several times, yet he was still prepared to come back. The second point is after coming back, he was issued with a new uniform and a gun. That's the 2nd of July, page 3. He was even issued with a new identity in 1993 and other false identity papers later which were in his possession when he was arrested. That's the 23rd of July, page 17. The next point is he said in the 1st of July interview, at the end of page 7, that he had no money and, therefore, had to stay with the parents of a waiter that he met in Sabac. At the end of page 11 of the same interview, he said that at the time he was in Sabac, he had 6.000 or 7.000 Deutschemarks with him. The next point is he claims he shot himself after returning to Brcko because he knew that they would want him to do more things. According to him, however, he had voluntarily returned to the area, and this occurred just after he had been given support from a certain high-ranking military officer to leave the SUP and work for that person. That's the 2nd of July, pages 3 and 4. He was even given a field vehicle, according to him, the one that he shot himself in. The 2nd of July, page 4. Mr. Jelisic said that he had 6.000 or 7.000 Deutschemarks -- sorry, this is the next point -- when he left Brcko. Even after buying a car that he said he bought, he would have had approximately 3.000 Deutschemarks left, which he claims he spent in two or three months. The average monthly income at the time, he agreed, would have been something in the order of 100 Deutschemarks or less. That's page 26 of the 1st of July. If he was really hiding out and wanting to be away from Brcko, I believe he would not have been spending the money on hotels, drink, and cigars, as he stated. In two or three months, he spent the equivalent of something like three years of salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. You also made the comment at the beginning of your evidence that he may have sanitised his account, but of course whether he did or not ultimately depends on the view the Trial Chamber takes of all the evidence that may be before them, and it's not necessary to go further into those matters because we looked at all the passages of the evidence upon which you would rely yesterday. One last question, and maybe I took you by surprise yesterday when I asked you about a particular witness -- a particular person. In fact, the name was given and is a name that's been given in evidence, so it's not a name that need be blanked out. There was a reference to a Dr. Ramic.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was he at the time -- is this the Dr. Ramic, do you know, who at the time was the brother of the senior political figure in the community, or is it a different Dr. Ramic, or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yesterday, I was asked if there was any corroboration to Mr. Jelisic's accounts that he saved a Dr. Ramic. I said, to a certain extent, I believe, in that he was still alive. I based that on the fact that I was aware that a Dr. Ramic from Brcko was interviewed and is, therefore, of course still alive. I did not speak to that person, as I said yesterday; that has been done since I moved on from the case. I, therefore, cannot say if it is the same Dr. Ramic or not; however, yesterday, I had a look at the statements and I cannot find any reference to any dealings with Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you wait, you'll be asked further questions.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. O'Donnell, just a few matters that I want you to deal with, please. In respect of matters of cooperation, would you accept this: that although he may have been unprepared to speak about some matters, there are some matters which would place him in a considerable amount of danger if he was to speak about certain people?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I believe that is the case, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you agree with this: that some of his diffidence about moving on to new characters, as it were, may have been based on his concerns about his safety and, perhaps more importantly, that of his family?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's a possibility, Your Honours. I can't comment on whether that was what was on his mind or not at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Next, please, the matters which he admitted and to which he has pleaded guilty to before the Tribunal. Would you agree with this: that having entered those pleas and made those admissions, those acts saved a considerable amount of other investigation which might have been necessary if he'd pleaded not guilty?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I do not actually believe that that is the case because of the status of the investigation when we spoke to Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Perhaps I can approach it in a slightly different way. If he had put forward, in relation to these matters to which he pleaded guilty and admitted, a bogus story, that would have entailed further investigation in order to undermine such a bogus story as he had put forward, would it not?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It could have, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. As far as information which you already knew, you did not tell him in advance what information you already had, did you?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, we did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So if he provided information to you which you already knew, it's not his fault that it's of limited value, is it?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've dealt with him as far as the information that he gave and you described it as being of limited value because of inconsistencies. Would you agree with this: that the limited value because of inconsistencies, that damages his value as a potential witness giving evidence before the Tribunal but does not necessarily devalue the quality of the actual information, does it?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's possible that leads of inquiry could still be generated from the information given. The matter goes towards the credibility of the information, I believe, as well as the potential for him to be a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If he gave information, are you in a position to say whether or not further inquiries have been made about that information and, without going into detail, whether that's revealed any further information of value?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not in a position to talk about inquiries arising from the information given to us by Mr. Jelisic; however, I can say that the information that has been given is of limited value to us, as I explained yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I appreciate that we haven't gone into the details of any names, but has the information that he gave led to further inquiries being made?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Not that I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How soon after interviewing him did you cease to be involved in the Jelisic case, completing the interviews last year?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Prior to the arrest of Mr. Jelisic, I had moved to other investigations. I returned to work briefly on this investigation mainly for the purpose of doing the interviews with Mr. Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: After you'd completed the interviews of Mr. Jelisic, you returned to your other duties outside this case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Is this correct, Mr. O'Donnell: During the course of investigations on the ground in Brcko, the drainage system at Luka facility was searched?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Part of the drainage system was searched. I can explain that in greater detail if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure if that's going to be necessary, but just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you don't mind, let the interpreters finish interpreting the question. Would you mind repeating it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The question was: "During the course of investigations on the ground in Brcko, the drainage system at Luka facility was searched." Perhaps you would like to repeat your answer, please, Mr. O'Donnell.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, part of the drainage system at Luka was searched. There were four --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No doubt, you are particularly interested in those, if I can call them, drains which witnesses had spoken about or given statements about concerning killings; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was it to those drains that the attention of the search was directed?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: To two of the four drains. There were four drains in the general area outlined by witnesses; two of those drains were searched, another one of the drains was covered in bitumen and we cannot access it, and the fourth drain was too deep and too narrow to be able to search.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you confirm that of the two drains that were searched, there was no evidence of human detritus found in those drains?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Do you mean human biological material?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Bones and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That is correct. The only point I would make is that there was one dental plate found in one of the drains.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Were you able to identify how long that dental plate had been in the drain?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, we were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Finally this, Mr. O'Donnell: I wish to draw to the attention of the Tribunal the comment that the defendant made about the theft of a coffee machine. Would you agree with this: that stealing a coffee machine falls into a rather different category from the killings of 12 or 15 people, Mr. O'Donnell?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I do agree that the theft of a coffee machine falls into a different category. I still believe that the answer given is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That, of course, is your opinion, but I think you've answered the question as to the relative merits of stealing coffee machines and killing 15 people. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A very limited number of questions, Mr. O'Donnell. In relation to anxiety or fear consequent on giving information, information of the type that might lead to further inquiries, would that be given on terms of confidentiality to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And any such information given on those terms, would it be kept confidential?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It would be kept confidential. The terms would be discussed with the person giving it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turning now to the value of the information provided, at the time it was provided to you, was it, although information you already had, surprising that this information should repose in this man, or was it information that was all but in the public domain, or what? Try and describe it in those terms.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: A lot of the information that was provided was in the public domain, on television, on videos, and details of people in positions in and around Brcko were also common knowledge to people who had spent some time in Brcko, particularly people who were there in the period just before the outbreak of war, such as witnesses, residents of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apart from that material, did he provide you with anything that was outside that general category?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: No, I do not believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were asked effectively whether the information provided led to the launching by the Office of the Prosecutor of any new inquiries. Not withstanding your change of function within the office, would you be aware of any new inquiries started as a result of that information provided?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Again, as you've emphasised, my knowledge is limited because I had no involvement in the case in recent times; however, one inquiry which was generated was checking Mr. Jelisic's version of events about a certain person he claimed that he saved. That person, I believe, has given evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Is that it? That's the only knowledge you have of further inquiries?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: There may have been some other general inquiries.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Basham may be able to help. Finally, the search of the drainage system, to the extent that there was such a search, was conducted in which year?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: This examination was conducted in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Four years after the events about which we're concerned.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Although one was covered in bitumen, had the other drains been apparently open to the elements in the intervening period of time?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. There were also a number of other items found in the drains.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What I'm going to do in relation to those, because Mr. Greaves hasn't had notice of them, is I'll ask you to tell me about them afterwards and after the session, and we can deal with them, if necessary, through Mr. Basham, but I don't want to take the Defence by surprise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No other questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Be careful here. This is the re-examination and the Defence cannot take the floor again. I don't want you to ask questions about which the Defence cannot answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not proposing to ask any more questions of this witness. The same topic can always be covered, if it's fair to do so, via Mr. Basham, but I'm not going to deal with it further through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me turn to Judge Riad. Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. O'Donnell.

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Riad, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I just want some clarifications or -- I want to understand more globally what you called the inconsistencies in your investigations, and if you can give me a clear answer, I would be very grateful. It appears, from your investigations, that Mr. Jelisic always affirmed that he received orders and he received lists and he was executing them, he was executing the orders. In your assessment, do you think that he also parallelly was the decision-maker in other killings and he did not give any account to anybody and he was not really compelled at all to do it, or was it, according to him, and he perhaps convinced you that he was just executing the orders?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Jelisic said that he only committed killings that he was told to commit. I believe that that is not the case. I believe that there were also killings which he himself decided to commit. We have a number of witnesses who, during the course of the investigation, have given us information on what appear to be random killings. One of the examples that I gave of a killing which was clearly not specifically ordered was the killing of Mr. Jasarevic, who was being held at the police station presumably for questioning and/or execution, who somehow managed to escape, but didn't get far before being stopped. Although he was stopped and surrounded by police and soldiers, Mr. Jelisic ran up to him, shot him in the head and killed him. He knew nothing about Mr. Jasarevic and had not been ordered to kill him. Yet rather than returning him to the police station, he simply executed him. There are a number of other witnesses who tell of apparently random killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What you call random killings was left to his whim completely, or was there some kind of common denominator which unites all these killings?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I believe that there is a common denominator, but the only common denominator that I can see is that the killings were of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned also that -- I quoted you -- "Others were always in charge of him." What's the meaning of "others were in charge of him"?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Jelisic claimed that he was told to commit the killings and was threatened with death if he didn't. He said that all of the killings he committed, he was ordered to, and that he did not have a position of authority. So he maintained that other people were in charge of his actions and other people were in charge of him at Luka camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: In fact, you mentioned that he said he had no option, either to kill or to be killed. Was this the impression you got from the investigation?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's true that Mr. Jelisic presented himself as a person who was faced with a decision to either kill or be killed himself. I believe that the details that I've mentioned in the inconsistencies show that that version of events is not believable. I do not believe that he only committed killings that he was ordered to commit, and I do not believe that he honestly thought he would be killed if he did not commit those killings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You also mentioned that he returned voluntarily to the killing, although he was offered to work with a high-ranking officer and avoid killing. Could you just give us more light on this?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Mr. Jelisic voluntarily returned to the area; not specifically to Brcko initially. He went to Bijeljina, but Bijeljina is about 40 kilometres away. Given that that was his hometown and that's where this all started, it's reasonable, I believe, to presume that he would go to Brcko or be sent to Brcko if he went back to Bijeljina. He did go to Bijeljina and was taken to Brcko, according to him. He said that he met there with a high-ranking military official. This is after he had been taken back to the police station and issued with a new uniform, new equipment, and another gun. He said that he was desperate -- these are my words, I'm sorry, I'm summarising -- he was desperate to avoid getting back into that, and he met with a senior military official, who greeted him, kissed him on the forehead, and told him words to the effect of he should not be upset and that he would try and help him out of this hell, as Mr. Jelisic put it. He told him that he should go to the SUP and tell them that he had to work with a high-ranking military official and that he could have nothing more to do with the SUP, in other words, with the killing and other activities. So it appears that there is finally light at the end of the tunnel. He's even given a military field vehicle. And yet when he finally does have a way out, he claims that he shoots himself in the leg to avoid having to do more killings. But again this is after he has voluntarily returned to the area. Of course, he's run out of money.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Just one last question. Did he cooperate with you in the investigations or did he give you misleading information?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I cannot say that Mr. Jelisic did not cooperate. He voluntarily took part in nine interviews, and he admitted to doing the actual killings. However, he did give us, I believe, a lot of incorrect information. He gave us a very sanitised version of events for those killings. Whenever we had a witness account saying that he did anything more than march someone along the street and pull a trigger, for example, someone pleading with him, begging for their life, he would say that that person was lying. That, combined with his basic statements that he only committed these killings because he was forced to and he would have been killed otherwise, and the inconsistent information he gave, which I believe shows those claims not to be credible, mean that he did not fully cooperate. His cooperation was very limited, in the true sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. O'Donnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Rodrigues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. O'Donnell, I think that most of the questions have already been asked, but I have a further one. You said that Mr. Jelisic came to Brcko voluntarily. However, the way that he saw things, in his own mind, in the beginning, do you believe that that matched or corresponded to the assignments that were asked of him, or is there any type of difference in that?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Could you repeat the question for me, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't clear. My question is to know the following: When somebody offered him the chance to go to Brcko, did those people explain to him what he was to do and, in fact, what he did was what those people had asked him to do, or after having arrived in Brcko, was there a change or a difference between what those individuals said to him at the beginning, what they offered him, and what he had to do? Do you understand what I mean now?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for interrupting you, because my question is the assertion that he came to Brcko voluntarily, yes, but in order to do what, if there is a difference between what he did and what he had in his mind that he was to do?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: It's very difficult, Your Honour, for me to answer that question, because the only account that I have of that is what Mr. Jelisic has told me. According to him, he was given some details before they went to Brcko, but initially his duties were different to what he was later doing. He was initially told that they would be met by certain officials and that there was a plan. It's difficult to know exactly what was in his mind at the time, because we have limited detail of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Rodrigues. Mr. O'Donnell, I only have a few questions to ask you, because some of the questions I wanted to ask have already been asked. About how much time or how many hours did you spend with Mr. Jelisic, because in the binder, the time is indicated, but approximately?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Approximately 25 to 30 hours, I would estimate, of interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twenty-five. So one could assume that you have a certain understanding of this person that you had in front of you. My question is the following: It's not the sentencing hearing, I understand that, but this is the only question I have. Throughout these interviews, during the 25 hours, did you feel any type of hatred or aversion towards the Muslims in Goran Jelisic or not at all?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's very difficult again to answer that, because Mr. Jelisic presented us with what he wanted us to believe. That's my opinion, and I've outlined what his position was, that he was forced to do the killings, et cetera. So from the interviews, when he talks about killing someone, he was talking about that person in terms of them being helpless and so forth, but he did not present to us hatred towards that person. In fact, he was trying to show the reverse, I believe, that he was not wanting to do that murder. So rather than saying, "I did it because I hated the person," he was saying, "I did not want to do that murder. I felt sorry for the person, but I was in the situation where I had to do it."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I didn't express myself correctly. Did you have the feeling that Goran Jelisic was the bearer of some kind of ideology, a political one, in respect of his country, or in respect of the area he came from or the war that was taking place, or in the end was all of that really something that didn't stay in his head and that he did what he had to do, somewhat in his own way, without an overall vision? Do you understand what I'm trying to get at?

utterances.speaker: BERNARD PATRICK O'DONNELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do understand what you are trying to get at. I would say that he did not come across in the interviews as someone who had a particular ideology that he was enforcing, but I have to clarify that by saying that I believe that he was going out of his way to show something very different to that. So it would be unreasonable, I believe, from the interviews, to get that picture. That's a picture that we could get from other places, other people who had had contact with him. But given the nature of the interviews, it did not come out, and I do not believe it could have come out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. O'Donnell, we would like to thank you for having made yourself available to the Prosecutor who called you. Since you're one of the investigators, I'm saying this for the public gallery. But this is all helpful to the Defence and to the Judges. You can now go back to your responsibilities within the Tribunal. You will be escorted, although you do know your way around here. We have another 20 minutes before we take our break, so we can move now to the next witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Give us your name and given name, your date and place of birth, and then your current occupation. Then take an oath, and after that, you may be seated. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my full name is Paul Anthony Basham. I was born on the 2nd of December, 1966 in New Zealand. I'm an investigator for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Basham. You may now be seated. Thank you for having come. You have been called by the Prosecutor as part of the trial initiated by the Office of the Prosecutor against Goran Jelisic, the accused, who is in this courtroom. I am not going to explain the proceedings to you; you are familiar with them. Mr. Nice, without any further ado, will ask you the questions that he wants to. Mr. Nice, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Basham, have you, over recent months or it may be a year or so, been the investigator in charge of this case?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, did you attend many of the interviews with the defendant, although the last witness, Mr. O'Donnell, was primarily the officer dealing with the interviews at that stage?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I only want you to deal with some photographs. Did photographs come into the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor in two ways? First, did some photographs come to the next witness, Mr. Ralston, and he, of course, made them available to you?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did other photographs and, indeed, a contact sheet, that is, a sheet showing a whole series of pictures from a film, come directly into your possession?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we go into private session for just a minute or so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will go into a very short private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Basham, the photographs that you're going to produce are in a series, and is it right that photographs from that series have been produced in magazines and books around the world?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. The photographs first appeared on the 9th of May, 1992 in a number of publications around the world. Since that date, they have continued to appear in magazines, newspapers, and, in one case, a television documentary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The photographs are collectively exhibited number of 67, and I would be grateful if they could now be provided to the witness and placed on the ELMO, and we'll deal with this in sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to point out to the public that these photographs are very difficult to look at, and anybody feeling particularly sensitive should leave the public gallery. You don't have to, but I would simply like to inform you and to advise you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we could go to the first photograph in the series, Mr. Basham, does this show the defendant on the right-hand side in the blue shirt carrying the gun, following two men down an alley or small road in Brcko, and at the end of that alley can be seen some other bodies already lying on the ground?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We can just check, for the assistance of the Tribunal, the location of this alley or lane later, but eventually, in what direction does it point?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: The laneway runs down towards the river, and the direction in which the people in the photograph are walking is the direction towards -- away from the SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's the police station?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: The police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next photograph, please. Does this photograph show the defendant shooting at a man in the brown pullover?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next photograph, please. In sequence and to a similar effect?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the left-hand side, at the bottom left-hand corner, can something be seen there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other man, already apparently shot and killed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next photograph, please. Later in the sequence, the man going towards the ground with bodies at the end of the small lane.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Next photograph, please. In sequence, the man now on the ground, the defendant still aiming at the man.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following photograph, please. Self-explanatory. The following photograph. A man on the ground, the defendant still aiming the gun towards the man.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following photograph. To the same effect?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And, indeed, the one after that in the sequence?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the one after that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next photograph turns to show a picture of the first man.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The last photograph in this sequence shows both men dead on the ground.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The remaining photographs show a mass grave, and you, as the investigating officer, know that there has already been evidence relating to these photographs that enables them to be linked to the exhumation of a mass grave some years later.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we move then, please, to the next photograph? Is this a view into a mass grave with the bodies and the way they've been thrown into the grave revealed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The following photograph. A different angle of the same.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next photograph shows the digging equipment, if we look at the top of the photograph --

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- that was plainly used to dig out the mass grave. It shows the same configuration of the bodies within the grave.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it also shows the side, at the top right-hand corner, of a lorry. We'll see a little more of the lorry in the next photograph, but what can you help us with -- it's not very clear -- the marking on the side of that lorry immediately behind the man?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: The marking to which you refer appears to be a flag or a sheet of some sort that has an emblem similar to, if not the same as, the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Over the page to the last -- not over the page -- to the last photograph, a little more of that lorry now to be seen, and there is evidence in the case, is there not, that the lorries used were refrigerated trucks from a particular local factory?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I promised that I would provide -- in relation to another topic, I promised I would provide some information to Mr. Greaves before he came to cross-examine this witness. If the usher would be good enough, I can provide it to him now, if that's acceptable to the Court. It's the only way of communicating when we're some metres away. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I suggest that we take a 20-minute break, and after that, we can resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will resume the hearing now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Two other questions of this witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First, Mr. Basham, in your capacity as investigating officer, are you aware that in the course of the drainage search at the Luka facility, there were things found in one of the grates or underneath one of the grates that had been identified as a grate where killings took place?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that it was cartridge casings, some six, and a bullet and a fragment of a bullet? Do you remember that or would you need to refer to records to confirm that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I do have a memory of that. It's been some time since I turned my attention to the actual document, but I think you're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second question which I ask you in order to make easier sense of the evidence coming from the next witness: The Chamber has been looking regularly at two lists of people, one a shorter list of 39 names, which has been fully explained to them, and the other a longer list of 100 names that, in the format the Chamber has had, have been set out alphabetically. Was that list of named individuals drawn from several documents that are going to be provided by the next witness, Mr. Ralston, which he had himself obtained from the local Serb authorities?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes. I had taken the names from those documents and put them into a spreadsheet for ease of use.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As we're going to see, those lists in fact identify a number of bodies, considerably larger than 100, but since many of the people could not be identified by name at all, it happened to be just 100 that could be named?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Will you wait there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Basham, I just want to ask you, please, about the items which were found in the drain. It cannot be said, can it, as to when those items found their way into that drain?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: No, I don't believe it can.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Nor who put them there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Or how they got to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That was going to be my next question. Thank you very much. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Judge -- excuse me. Mr. Nice, excuse me. It was so fast that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Nothing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I was going faster than you are. Excuse me. Do you have a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, nothing from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Riad, you had a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Basham.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Perhaps you can help me understand something which appears very bewildering to me. We have here at least ten pictures which I wondered how they were taken. It is pictures taken of an execution, step by step. How can a person who is killing in this way take a photographer with him to picture it? It almost sounds like a head of state going to a conference and having his pictures taken. We can see the man being killed in the second picture standing, and then he's killed halfway, and then he's killed three quarters, he's killed on the ground, and then he's killed while being dead, and at a very short distance. I mean I'm astonished to see how such pictures could be taken while it's happening. Do you have any interpretation for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Forgive my interrupting. It may be easier for the witness to answer this question in private session. I think it probably would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, private session. I would like to remind all the parties here that the confidential elements regarding the photographer's identity must remain confidential and not be revealed to the outside, not revealed outside this courtroom, for the safety of the person who took the photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in private session now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next and last witness is available. I say "last witness" with one caveat, which I will deal with after the evidence is closed today. It's John Ralston.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please remain standing for a few moments. Give us your name, your given names, your date and place of birth, your current position and residence, and then we will ask you to take an oath, and then please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My full name is John Hunter Ralston, R-A-L-S-T-O-N. I'm the chief of investigations at the International Tribunal, and my address is the Tribunal address, Churchillplein 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take the oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated now. Thank you for having come to the trial which has been initiated by the Office of the Prosecutor, of which you are a member, the trial of the accused Goran Jelisic. Mr. Nice is going to ask you a few questions, and I won't explain the proceedings any further to you, since you are well familiar with them. Mr. Nice, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honours, in this case, for this witness, there has been prepared a comprehensive bundle of exhibits which I think is going to be given a number, or has already been given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This will be Prosecution Exhibit 68 for Mr. Ralston's statements and Exhibit 69 for the materials that were just passed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's also a map which can be produced at some stage that has become Exhibit 70.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Exhibit 70 will be the number for the map.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, has your intended evidence been reduced to a summary, and is that a summary that you have read and that you adopt as accurate?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That is, indeed, Exhibit 68. Dealing briefly with relevant background, you started with the Office of the Prosecutor here in June 1994, being promoted to the position of chief of investigations in April of 1998, in that position having overall responsibility for the direction and management of all investigations undertaken by this office.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And through that work, have you developed a diverse understanding of the circumstances, chronology, events, individuals, and groups relevant to the armed conflicts in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we look, please, at the map, Exhibit 70? There's a larger-scale version for the members of the Court and, indeed, for the witness but a conveniently small one that will fit on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Using the pointer in the way that you will be familiar, if you acquire it, just explain the different colours and what this map shows in a couple of sentences.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: The colours of the map, I think, if you look at this area here [indicates] is Bosnia-Herzegovina. The area in red is the area which is now Republika Srpska. The areas in the yellow and green are what is now the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Posavina region is situated, I think, in the northern extremity of this map. Can you just indicate that in general terms?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Posavina is, in general terms, this area here [indicates], the Drina going down there, the Sava along there, the Bosna down here somewhere, and the Majevica mountains across here [indicates], and then you have this plain here which is generally the Posavina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that's a fertile, flat plain, I think?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The corridor, as it's described, from Brcko to Bosanski Samac, can you point that out to us?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think that's this area along here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It occupies most of or the northern part of that fertile plain, and the majority of the inhabitants are concentrated or were concentrated in the towns of Brcko and then Orasje and Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Historically, can you tell us something from your researches or knowledge of what happened in the Second World War and what is, as it were, remembered from the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Okay. In this area, there were numerous atrocities carried out by the Ustasha, mainly against the Serbs in the area, particularly around Brcko and Doboj, and those areas. At the same time, there were atrocities being committed against the Muslims -- Bosnian Muslims in Bosnia during World War II. What this meant is that the Bosnian Muslims were unlikely to join in with the resistance, the Serb resistance to the Ustasha, and in fact several of them were actually members of the Ustasha. I think towards the latter part of the war, a German Handzar division came across, I think, from various locations over in Serbia, and again Bosnian Muslims were recruited into the Handzar division. Following that distribution, it became notorious for atrocities committed against the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there, indeed, in Brcko a memorial, or is that something that's outside your detailed knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I believe there is a memorial in Brcko, but I don't have too much detail of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was Brcko economically a very developed community and an economic and cultural centre for the area?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've seen some photographs showing railway lines and we've seen a map. Was it a hub, really, for both railroad and river transportation?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, it was, and I think that in the larger version of the map, it should be evident that those forms of transport were available and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry. With its proximity to Croatia, once you crossed the bridge, you were only a comparatively small distance from the main trading route, the main road trading route running through that part of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes. There's a highway that runs across the top here to Zagreb, and you, of course, can travel from there across to Belgrade or up towards Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The river, as we have heard, was crossed by two bridges; one, a general road bridge and the other a rail bridge.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By both those means, it was possible to connect with this general transportation system a little further north?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct. It was also connecting from the areas down here [indicates] in other parts of Bosnia, in what's now the Federation territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 11, you set out in your summary statistics of population composition for 1991, many of them, if not nearly all of them, have already been given. So in summary, this: At that time, Brcko was predominantly a Muslim town with a majority of some 55 per cent being Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The other statistics are set out, if that's of assistance. How important was Brcko and this Posavina corridor to all the sides in the course of this conflict?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: It was one of the major areas of strategic importance. If you look at your map here again, this area in the red is the area that the Bosnian Serbs sort of control and, in fact, the area extended down here [indicates] and linked up with Croatia. In these areas in Croatia, you also had an autonomous Serbian republic proclaimed. So for the Serbian side, it was important to control this area here [indicates] so that it could link this part of the Republika Srpska with this part here [indicates] and also the Serbian regions around here. It was equally important, I think, for the Bosniak and the Croat sides who saw this area as its link across to the rest of Eastern Europe, but more importantly, if they could sever this link, then they obviously had a strategic advantage in isolating this area of the Serb-controlled lands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Tuzla? Just locate it for us, and what can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Tuzla, I think, is roughly about there [indicates]. That was a major industrial centre in this part of the territory, with salt mines and chemical factories, and the like. If this particular entity were able to control the corridor, then their access to this part of Europe was quite simple; otherwise, they were then forced to come by a very circuitous route down here, either to the city or up, and then back up and around. So if they were able to get control of this area, it would have been of quite a lot of significance for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So from all points of view, Brcko was an important strategic place?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On the 30th of April, 1992, did Serb forces from Bosnia and Herzegovina and elsewhere take action in respect of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you characterised the steps that, from your researches, were taken in Brcko, and can you just list them, please?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I think, leading up to the 30th of April, after the cessation of hostilities in Croatia, JNA forces withdrew into Bosnia to places where there were JNA barracks. One of those barracks was in Brcko, and various combat units and various pieces of equipment were moved to the barracks in Brcko. Similarly, in the lead up to the 30th of April, the Serb members of the local government demanded the area be divided up into three areas, including one area which would be an exclusive Serb section. This action led to, I think, quite intense negotiations between the parties. Then on the 30th -- on the evening or the night of the 30th of April, the bridges across the Sava River were blown up, thus cutting off any ability to cross the river there, and then the next day, an SDS-controlled crisis staff assumed control over the area within the municipality. The crisis staff, they then assumed control over all the key installations. They issued ultimatums over the radio for Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats who may have -- Croats who may have possessed arms, that they were to surrender them within two days; if they didn't surrender any weapons they possessed, that there would be shelling of the non-Serb areas. Shelling did, in fact, follow there. In some of the areas which were predominantly Muslim, there was some instantaneous type of resistance from those who possessed arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had the Serb forces seized control of any of the principal buildings as well?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, they had. They seized control of the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the translation and pause between question and answer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Certainly. Yes, they did seize control of some of the main buildings, including the post office, the radio and TV station, the hospital, the police buildings, and other key buildings in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Carrying on at a slightly slower speed, please, Mr. Ralston, picking it up, if you would be so kind, from about the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: From about the 2nd of May, as I said, there was some resistance in the predominantly Muslim areas which didn't prove to be effective against the organised forces that were against them. There was shelling against many of the houses and buildings in those neighbourhoods. Many of the civilians sought refuge in basements of homes, their own homes or homes of their neighbours. Then on the 3rd of May, Serb forces, JNA forces, the militias, the paramilitary then went through the various areas, residential areas and ethnically cleansed the non-Serbs from those areas. The people who were moved out of these areas were then taken to various collection centres. The non-Serb military-aged men were separated from the other people and then detained in places, such as the mosque, the Laser Bus Company, the JNA barracks, the Partizan Sports Hall, and the Luka facility. While this was going on, men were being taken to the police building where they were interrogated, and in the course of those interrogations, many of the non-Serb men were beaten, tortured, and many were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to interrupt you just for a couple of points. First of all, when was the date, so far as is known, of the establishment of the Luka facility?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: From the information that I have, it was established on the 7th -- around the 7th and 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When it comes to interrogations, and of course the Judges have already heard quite a lot of evidence about all this, but was there evidence of -- in most general terms, was there evidence of selection by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, there was. People were selected on the basis that they were Muslim. This was a subject of interrogations. People who were detained and taken out and murdered were done so on the basis that they were Bosnian Muslim. In the questioning and interrogation, accusations regarding their involvement in resistance and membership of the SDA were also quite often used as a pretext for the executions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you've run through that list of events in Brcko, and of course in the centre of that, there was -- though we haven't focused on it in this trial, there was shelling of the town.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you have an idea, not necessarily detailed at the moment, but an idea of the date range for the shelling of the town?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes. From around the 2nd of May until the 7th or 8th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To what extent does that picture of events that you have painted for us in respect of Brcko fit with events elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: These events didn't happen in isolation. In and around the same time period, similar events were occurring at various locations up and down Eastern Bosnia and across -- and shortly after that, across here [indicates] in the area that's known as the Bosanska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you say "similar events," are you restricting your observation to, for example, just detention and killings, or are you saying that there were similarities to the general buildup and the step-by-step process that was followed here?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes. I'm talking about the step-by-step process, the establishment of the crisis staff, the issuing of ultimatums, the artillery attacks on areas that the Serb forces wanted to control, the ethnic cleansing of various areas where the population was a non-Serb majority, the separating out and the torturing and beating and killing of men, particularly military-aged men, and their incarceration in centres of detention, so the full range of conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you produce some documents that deal with preparations that may have been made for, not necessarily these particular events, but events of this general category?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, if it's desired, as I think it may be, to lay some or all of these documents on the ELMO, they're all from Exhibit 69, and we can deal with them conveniently by reference to the numbered tabs. I think in all cases there are original French and English versions, but with the Chamber's leave, we'll just perhaps display the English version. This is tab 1, in English, the second sheet, the French being at the third sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is this, Mr. Ralston, the English translation of a document of which we have the original, dated the 15th of August, 1991, from the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia-Herzegovina's president, whose name is at the foot of the document, Karadzic, and explain the significance of one or two passages in this document, remembering that others may be following it in French? Will you identify the paragraph numbers if you turn to them?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes. As you ask, this is an English language translation of the document which precedes it. The significance, to me, of this document, if you'll note the date, the 15th of August, 1991, at that stage, it's a document issued from the president of the Serbian Democratic Party to all SDS municipal boards, and it's a document which sets out how they're organising, how the party should operate in each of the municipalities. It sets out at point 1 that municipal boards should meet once a week. Each week, they must review the situation in the local board for the past week. So in the municipal board of each municipality, there are various villages and towns where there are local boards. The local boards also should meet once a week, and every member of a local board must be entrusted with, at point 4, maintaining contact with 10 to 20 homes. So what it means, at this stage, the SDS was attempting to make sure that it could reach into basically every home where Serbs were and that information could be communicated backwards and forwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Shall we turn to tab 2? The original document comes first; again in the English version, second; in the French version, third. Is this a document, dated the 19th of December of 1991 from the Serbian Democratic Party's main committee, expressed to be instructions for the organisation and activities of the organs of the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we turn, in the English version, to the first sheet, which is broadly reflected in the French version but the French is in a larger typeface and goes on to one further sheet, but if we look at it in the English for these purposes, can you summarise, or taking in as much detail as is appropriate, paragraphs 1 to 4?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraphs 1 to 4 basically set out the conditions under which the following instructions are to be implemented. I think the first point is in point number 1, it talks about uniformed tasks and measures and activities developed which would be carried out within the national community of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in order to further implement the plebiscite decision whereby the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina decided to live in a single state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you only for the purpose of reminding you to speak more slowly when reading, even though I hope that the translation booths will be have been able to find the version that they may wish to read from. So leaving a break after I conclude this interjection, can you pick it up, but whenever reading, read a little more slowly?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Certainly. Basically, the plebiscite which was conducted in, I think, October of 1991 dealt with the question of the Serb people wanting to remain within the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or what is now the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. If we move to the second point on the document, it deals with the tasks and measures to be implemented basically for the readiness of the defence of the interests of the Serb people. The third point -- the significant part about the third point in the document -- I sorry, in the preface, I think, is this area here. There are two different sets of instructions, one set of instructions for municipalities where the Serb people are the majority, and the second set of instructions for the people in municipalities where the Serb people are not a majority, and which is the case in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed, in Brcko, the Serbs were a minority, because the Muslims alone were over 50 per cent and there were Croats and others, as well as Serbs, in the minority?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we turn then to that which is appropriate to municipalities where the Serb people are not a majority, we are looking for what's described as Variant B, in the English version we have to turn over two sheets for that to page 270653, and in the French version, we have to turn over to what is numbered page 5 at the bottom or 842555 at the top. Where I've taken you, Mr. Ralston, is the beginning of the instructions in relation to Variant B. Having located that point, is it later paragraphs, and I think numbers 9 and 10, that you would like to focus on?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, it is.
