I think the first comment with Variant B, it basically sets out the instructions for how they would operate the municipality or in such a municipality, and there are various relevant instructions in there. I go back to point 3 on the first page first, which is, in the English, page number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I gave one incorrect -- I'm sorry to interrupt you. I gave one incorrect page number for the French version. It starts at page 6, and it's on page 6, or alternatively page 842556, that the Chamber can find that which you're referring to. Paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 sets out that the municipality committee of the SDS will immediately form a crisis headquarters, and then goes on to detail who, beyond that headquarters, and then the functions that follow. If you come down to paragraphs 9 and 10, it sets out some of the preparations that should be taken in these municipalities; paragraph 9 dealing with the people of Serb nationality, to remain in the area, not to travel abroad, and paragraph 10, if you look at the subparagraphs, it deals with the role of the armed forces of the JNA, and reinforcing war units, and the relationship between those people and the SDS officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, we didn't focus on this, but the crisis community was said to be a -- crisis headquarters was to be a crisis headquarters of the Serb people in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I interrupted you. Would you like to go on beyond paragraph 10 and then go to what's called the second level, which can be found in the French version at page 8 or 842558?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Each of the paragraphs is obviously significant, but I draw your attention to paragraph 2 and paragraph 3 and then what follows paragraph 4. Basically, this deals with getting the -- having the military in a state of readiness and being mobilised, and the relationship, to some extent, between the military and the Territorial Defence unit and the SDS crisis committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then paragraph 7, I think.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Paragraph 7 sets out that the crisis headquarters is responsible for special forms of defence organisation in the areas where the Serbs are not a minority. It sets out that the headquarters is obliged to continually monitor the situation, the development of political and military and the security situation in the broader sense. The crisis headquarters is responsible for initiating and implementing activities that are suitable for every specific situation; that is to say, for an assessment of the possible development of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this document was issued in December 1991, but are you aware that the defendant Jelisic, in his interviews, makes reference to crisis staffs and their responsibly and authority as of May 1992?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The development of events in Brcko and in the other areas of which you've spoken, to what extent, in your judgement, did it match that which was set out as a general plan of operations in this document?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: My observations, from the material that we've gathered, is that the development of the situation in the various other areas matched that as set out in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we turn next to tab 3, the original, followed by English, followed by the French at 0407955, this being a letter to all the presidents of municipalities, dated March the 23rd of 1992, and signed by the president of the Serbian Democratic Party, Dr. Karadzic. On the English version, turning to the second paragraph, does it read as follows: "Taking into consideration that one of the essential conditions for the protection of Serbian people in the situation that has been created requires rapid and timely transfer of data and information relevant to our defence and security, as well as transfer of decisions, directions, and instructions made by the governing bodies. We have established a Republican operations centre and decided that in addition to the regional centre in Banja Luka, the following municipality centres take over the function of regional centres"? Does it then list a number of places, including Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Looking at the listed names, would Bijeljina be the nearest to Brcko or not, or can't you be sure?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: In my view, it would be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you then, please, just deal with any other particular significance in this document marked, as we see, to be destroyed after reading, and in particular with the paragraph that -- the next paragraph but one?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think the significance of this document is it deals with the whole communication issue. Firstly, it talks about the establishment of communication centres which match the autonomous regions which were established, and then in the paragraph commencing "The municipalities", it talks about how the various municipalities will communicate with these regional centres. And thus you have not only communication between the regions but between the municipalities within the regions to the regional headquarters, and then from there, presumably to the Republic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. In summary, between March and December of 1992, in the areas that you've been speaking of and to which these pieces of correspondence may have been directed, were there killings by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In towns, cities, villages?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in what numbers?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think the killings are best described as in thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that both of Muslims and of Croats?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Certainly, thousands of Muslims. I couldn't put a figure on Croats, but Croats were killed as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was there the rounding up of people, on the basis of ethnic or religious identities, and detention?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were there, to your knowledge, a number of Serb-operated detention camps?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you name -- and if necessary, perhaps we could have the map back, please. If you could point out the place. Could you name and, if possible, point out some of the other camps operated by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Camps KP Dom in Foca, which I think is down here somewhere [indicates]. If we come up to this area, to Vlasenica, we have Sesici [phoen] camp [indicates]. Up in this area around Zvornik [indicates], you would have Celopek camp. I think there were one or two other camps there as well, Karakaj Secondary Technical School. If you come over into this area [indicates], you have the camps of Omarska, Keraterm, Trnopolje, and Manjaca, you also had camps in municipalities in Kljuc, in Kotor Vares, or detention facilities in those areas [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From your reading of the material relating to these other camps and including Brcko, was there any particular focus of attention on any segment or segments of the Bosnian Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, there was. Well, anybody who was a Muslim was a target for abuse. It's more pronounced against the leadership and senior and prominent officials within the Bosnian Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Intellectuals and professionals, were they dealt with just the same as everyone else, or were they selected for special treatment?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: They were targeted for interrogations and beatings and killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That pattern throughout the area, so far as Brcko is concerned, did that fit with the general pattern or was it in conflict with the general pattern?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: It fitted with the general pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At some stage in the interview, one of his interviews, the defendant spoke of the selection of people by being prominent. Does that fit with the general pattern?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were these activities widespread and involving the killing of the thousands of people you've spoken of?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I turn to a different topic, documents relating to the mass graves of which we have had evidence in this case. Paragraph 28 of the summary. On the 9th of December, Mr. Ralston, did you receive certain documents?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 4 is the first of these documents?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From whom did you receive them?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I received them from a man named Goran Neskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: His role being --

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: At that stage, he was a Deputy Minister of Justice for the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To what did those documents relate?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: They related to a -- what do you call it -- a review by a man named Avlijas of prisons and collection camps on the territory of Republika Srpska. The documents indicate that Mr. Avlijas was asked to go and survey the various facilities that existed, and he prepared a report, and the documents include that report that he prepared on the facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you meet the man Slobodan Avlijas a couple of days later on the 11th of December?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he authenticate the documents?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we look at the first one, tab 4? If that can go on the ELMO. Thank you. This is effectively a covering document from the Republika Srpska's Ministry of Justice and Administration at Pale, dated the 22nd of October of 1992, with the distribution list set out, but this document saying, "Please find enclosed a report on the situation in prisons and collection camps for prisoners of war on the territory of Republika Srpska, supervised and inspected by this Ministry." It says that it will take all appropriate measures stipulated by law to remove shortcomings?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we turn, please, to document 5, the English version coming second, the French version starting at page 0068287. If we put the English first sheet -- thank you very much -- on the ELMO, is this the report of the man Avlijas, dated the 22nd of October, headed "Report", and saying, in the introduction, this: "On the basis of a list of prisons and camps for prisoners of war submitted by the International Red Cross on the orders of the Government of Republika Srpska and the relevant ministry, in the period from 10 to 17 October 1992, I conducted inspections and conversations with responsible organs in the following place ..."? Does the document then go on to deal with other locations, so that we can turn over a sheet to number 3, which is Brcko?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you read, please, remembering the speed that is appropriate, what was said in the report about Brcko?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: "In the town of Brcko or its environs there is no prison or camp for the temporary accommodation of detained enemy soldiers. "I visited this town to verify a report by the International Red Cross whose content was alarming. It said that a large number of citizens of Muslim nationality (the figure quoted was about 2,500 people) had been liquidated in that town. "I held a meeting with the most responsible people in Brcko (the president of the Municipality, the president of the Executive Board and the deputy in the Assembly of Republika Srpska). I checked and ascertained that in the immediate vicinity of the town (a suburb) there are five mass graves where a total of 226 people are buried, of whom 17 died of natural causes. These people died during combat activities in Brcko. Since there was the danger of an epidemic, these people were buried with religious rites at the said sites, at least according to their statements. The relevant services of the Interior Ministry and other services carried out the identification of the dead people on several occasions. "Documentation is enclosed herewith. "On that occasion, I learned that in the Brcko area there was a mass grave containing the bodies of 36 Serbian fighters. It is assumed that there are also mass graves of Muslims who buried their fighters during the retreat. "I suggested, and those present agreed, that the said graves be put in order and marked according to the regulations stipulated by the international law of war; that they be fenced in, that the documentation be preserved and that it be suggested to international organisations, should they insist, that the exhumation of corpses, their identification and the determination of the causes of death be carried out in the presence of an international arbitration commission and representatives of both warring parties."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Insofar as this report says at the previous page in the English version, and at the foot of that page, that people in the graves died during combat and were buried in accordance with religious rites, how does that fit with the photographs of how the bodies were deposited in the grave, the evidence of the findings of the bullet holes in the heads, or the rest of the evidence that we have presented to this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: To me, it doesn't fit with people having died in combat activities. Indeed, some of the bodies removed, I think we have evidence, they were actually killed after being interned in the Luka camp. The wounds on some of the bodies did not indicate that they were a result of combat activities, and I think the photograph of the bodies being dumped in the grave that we attended indicate that there weren't religious rites being observed at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He says in that same passage that he met the most responsible people in Brcko and then sets out some office holders. Just yes or no to this question: Do you now know by name any of those office holders or not?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we go into private session very briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we now go to tab 6, and is this the first of the documents that were annexed to Avlijas' report and authenticated by him?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tab 6 perhaps needs just a little clarification. It is a small piece of paper, which we can see in the original at the first page of tab 6, which is translated simply in the English version that is on the ELMO, in the French version at 00686293. It is the passage to be found in the top right-hand corner, and the rest of the page was a separate sheet. It's simply the way the document has been dealt with. This single sheet of paper read that "From 1 May 1992 to 10 July 1992, buried in a mass grave were 216 persons in total, 103 identified, 8 died of natural causes," and there were "9 female bodies. As of 10 July 1992, the people killed were buried at a cemetery, properly marked and with religious rites." So that's simply a piece of paper that was part of this report.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we then go to tab 7, do we find the first of several lists associated with the report, and it may help just briefly to look at the original of this, the first sheet of this, just on this occasion. We see that there were lists by number. Sometimes there are names given with other details; sometimes, as we're going to see when we look at the translations, there were no details given. But the original version itself had names and some details on it; is that right, Mr. Ralston?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So if we look at then, for the convenience of non-speakers of B/C/S, the English version, the French version following at 00686293, do we find a document dated the 5th of May, 1992, and then the first 16 names -- sorry, the first 16 items are names, the remaining 17 to 33 are simply described as an unknown person, either female or male, of a particular age?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Chamber may see on this document some familiar surnames at any event. If we turn then to tab 8, we are going to see effectively a similar format, although there has been some overcopying from one page to the next, but the original document is a separate sheet for the 6th of May and contains 14 items. The English and French versions --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think something has gone wrong with the French version, for which I apologise. I'm very grateful to Ms. Reynders, who is always on top of the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In the French version, at page 686294, the Chamber is concerned with the first 15 names only, and these are names, or at least there are 13 names, dated the 6th of May, and two unidentified bodies.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes. There are 15 items on the list, but there are two number 14s on the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much. Number 9, tab number 9 is a longer list, going up to 169. The English version starts at 4613, the French version at 6294. As we can see, there are sequentially lists for the 6th of May, the 9th of May, a very long list, the 10th of May, the 11th of May, and then shorter lists between the 12th of May and the 4th -- I beg your pardon, the 10th of July, eventually the 30th of June and the 10th of July?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have almost concluded what I wished to ask this witness. I simply note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What do you want to ask? I see there is one more document, number 10. Do you have questions to ask after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I should deal with that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But after this document, are you finished or do you have other questions to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No. I will be finished after this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then we are going to finish. I think that would be better. We can begin the cross-examination after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Turn, please, then to tab 10 and just tell us about that document, if you can. This is a document dated the 12th of May of 1992, so it's in the middle of or immediately after the events with which we are immediately concerned.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: This document comes out of the Official Gazette from the Republika Srpska National Assembly. I think the significant point on this document is point 2, which sets out that one of the strategic objectives or priorities of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina is to "set up a corridor between Semberija and Krajina." Semberija and Krajina are the two areas adjacent to the Posavina corridor on the western side of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the eastern side of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That does conclude all I need to ask of this witness. The Chamber will recall at an earlier stage that we've heard that some of the names of victims known to this Court through evidence are also to be found on those lists. If it would be helpful, I can pinpoint them for you immediately after the adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's almost five after one. I want to thank the interpreters, of course, and we will resume at 2.30 for the cross-examination. Court stands adjourned. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.02 p.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume the hearing. Please have the accused brought in, and be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody is here. Does everybody hear me? All right. We can begin the cross-examination of the chief of the investigating department at the OTP. Mr. Greaves, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Ralston, can I just go to, if I may call it, your report, your witness summary, at paragraph 6, please. I just want to deal with a couple of details, fairly quickly, of historical matters. In that paragraph, you describe Brcko. Is this also right, that Brcko actually fell within the state which was set up by the German occupiers, the State of Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's not within my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As far as paragraph -- also paragraph 6, the atrocities to which you refer in there were not only directed by -- I'm sorry. Let me just put this again. They were not only just Serb atrocities at that stage, the Croatians were also involved in anti-Muslim atrocities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: As I understand it, no, that it was basically Serb atrocities towards -- there were Serb atrocities towards Muslims, and there were Croatian atrocities towards Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And indeed there's a monument at Luka facility, you may be aware of this, which deals with Croatian atrocities against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The Muslims at that stage didn't form part of the Ustasha regime; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: They didn't form part of the regime, but as I understand it, there were Muslims who were part of the Ustasha.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The unit which you've referred to as the Handzar division, that in fact, for sake of clarity, was in fact an SS division, wearing and supported by the SS organisation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And they carried out widespread and significant atrocities against the Serbs in the latter part of the war?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Paragraph 8, please. You have dealt with the importance of Brcko, and I just want to add one or two matters to that, if I may, please. It's right, isn't it, that Bosnia-Herzegovina lacks, on the Adriatic coast, any real port which it could use?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: It has access to the coast in one very small area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. It's a very small, tiny port, not the sort of port that you would use for large amounts of commerce?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you could or you couldn't, but it is a very limited area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. That limitation enhances, does it not, the importance of Brcko as a strategic location to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The alternative route which you have described for exports and imports, so effectively going around the area occupied by the Republika Srpska, if that was the only one available, it would make importing and exporting to Eastern Europe an almost unrealistic, uneconomic proposition, would it not?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I don't know if it would make it unrealistic or uneconomic. It would certainly make it more difficult and more time-consuming.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The importance of Brcko led, did it not, to the establishment of an international arbitration commission to determine its future?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I don't think it's correct to say the importance of Brcko led to that. It was the one area that they were unable to settle in the Dayton Agreements, and so -- because both parties to that agreement claimed rights to Brcko, and that's what led up to the arbitration.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But both sides were anxious to have it, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In that sense, because both sides were anxious to have it and weren't prepared to agree on it at Dayton, it became important because of that, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I don't think I would agree with you in terms when you said it was important. It was, it was important to both sides, and both sides wanted to have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You set out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I'm losing the interpretation here. All right, please proceed. Yes, the French booth is back in business.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Mine has gone very faint for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You set out, Mr. Ralston, in your summary, the advantages to each side. Those, in essence, are the reasons why people were not prepared to agree to give it to the other side and why it was sufficiently important for it to be put to an international commission; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think they are some of the reasons. I think one of the other reasons was that some of the non-Serb population were the majority in that area prior to the conflict, and they wanted to resettle in that area, and had the area come under Serb control, they viewed at that stage it would be very difficult. And on the Serb side, on the other hand, I believe that they were of the view that they had to control that, and if 55 per cent of the population was Muslim, they wouldn't be able to control that part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The result of that commission, I think, came out in the spring of this year, and it's now, I think, a 20-year international control has been recommended.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's, in essence, what's occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The process by which the commission conducted its work, was it, in part, by receiving evidence from the various parties?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you agree with this? And if you don't know the answer, please tell us. Was it right that part of the case laid before the commission by Bosnia-Herzegovina sought to demonstrate, to prove, that genocide had, in fact, taken place in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I haven't read the case they put forward, so that's outside my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All right. Can you help us, please, about this? It may be just a matter of phraseology. If you look, please, at paragraph 13(1), the final two lines, please, in the English version you refer to the "greater Serbian nations", with the words "greater" and "nations" having lower case and not capitals. Could you just explain that phrase, please?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think what we're getting at there, they were basically -- there was a move to have all Serb territory in one body as part of Serbia, if you like, but you had the autonomous region of Serbian Krajina in Croatia, you had the Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then you had Serbia and as part of the Republic of Yugoslavia, and it's the combination of those three.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I now take you to what in the English version is page 4, and it's part of paragraph 14, and you go into some subparagraphs which are not numbered. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: On page 4, the second of those, and I'll just read it out, if I may. "In the spring of 1992, Serb members of the local government demanded that Brcko be divided into three areas, including an exclusive Serb section. The Serbian insistence led to negotiations between the parties." Were you aware of the context in which that took place which -- namely this, that about six weeks before fighting broke out, there had been a meeting in Lisbon of the various political leaders of Bosnia-Herzegovina; were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That was a meeting sponsored by and under the auspices of the European Community?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was a declaration signed at that meeting by all the parties, and by that I mean the parties from the various ethnic groups, a declaration was signed which set out the principles for the future constitutional arrangements for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was signed by all of the parties. I'd have to refresh my memory from the document, if you have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But you would accept that what was being discussed were the principles for the future constitutional arrangements?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think the discussions were based on a learning conflict, and there were some rather-pressing resolutions put forward which were seen to be averted. I think the critical thing is that didn't -- what was resolved at the Lisbon conference ultimately didn't occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I accept that, but would you accept this, that the broad proposition was for sovereign rule within its current borders, there being separate political entities and institutions for each national ethnic unit?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't accept that without reference to the document. I think that there was a complex proceeding, there was a complex document, so -- and it's not a document I've seen in recent times, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you accept that it was, in fact, subsequently and shortly thereafterwards [sic] repudiated by Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I'm sure it was repudiated by Alija Izetbegovic or his parliament.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The paragraph on the next page, the top paragraph, please, Mr. Ralston, you refer there to Bosnian Muslim men with light arms. By "light arms", do you mean modern military light arms?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: A range of things from shotguns and rifles. Their access to modern military equipment was extremely limited, from the information that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can we then go, please, to the next paragraph but one, and you use the phrase there "began to ethnically cleanse non-Serbs from Brcko hamlets and neighbourhoods". Could you give us your definition, please, of "ethnic cleansing"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: What I mean by that statement there is that the Serb forces would go from house to house and basically force the non-Serb population out of their homes. If they didn't go voluntarily, it wasn't uncommon for people to be ill-treated or even killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I put to you a series of stages, which you may or may not agree with as being a proper reflection of the generality of these incidents? Firstly, forced evacuation of the civilian population as stage 1; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Whether it's stage 1 or not, but it's certainly a characteristic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Then followed by the collection of those evacuees in various locations, often, for example, in Brcko, the barracks, or whatever?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Then after that, the separating out from those collective people of women, children, and men of military age.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And also of people of Serb ethnicity who considered themselves Serb nationals.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I don't think people of Serb ethnicity were caught up in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: We've heard some evidence in the case, Mr. Ralston, about people of Serb nationality having been separated from these groups.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: It's not that -- that's not within my knowledge, from the material that I've read.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The next stage was the evacuation of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you speak a little more slowly, please, a little bit of delay in between the questions and the answers? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As a next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know it's fast. Please proceed. Let the interpreter finish interpreting your question. Is everybody up to where we have to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As a next stage, Mr. Ralston, the evacuation of those women, children, and men of military age to locations away from Brcko, often in areas controlled by Bosnian Muslim authorities.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Again, we've heard evidence in the case about people being moved to various towns, some of them controlled or behind Muslim lines, but you're --

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, some people were. But in your question, you included every category of person we were talking about, and quite clearly, not every category of person was evacuated to behind military -- or to Muslim-controlled areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Which group of those do you say were not, in fact, evacuated?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Particularly, men between the ages of, say, 15 and 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. It may be that I didn't ask the question right, and I see that I didn't. I apologise. Let me just make it plain what I was suggesting. The evacuation of women and children and men of non-military age -- it's my fault entirely for a sloppy question, Mr. Ralston -- would you accept that as a proposition, that those groups were evacuated to various places?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Some of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Some were allowed to return to their homes?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thereafter, there was a continued detention of men of military age, and many of those, but not all, were in fact released.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Some were released, and they were subsequently recaptured, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of those who were not released, it's plain that some were killed, but those who were not killed and who remained in detention were subsequently moved to a place called Batkovic; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Batkovic was then, in turn, subsequently closed and people were either released or exchanged.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Batkovic operated for a considerable time after these events. I think it may have been operated up until 1994, but then from Batkovic, there were prisoner exchanges, and ultimately it was closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you accept this: There was a period in May 1992 when the entire Muslim or Bosniak population of Brcko was either detained by or under the control of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think it's difficult to say that the entire population was detained or controlled by, but certainly a very large percentage of it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What would you say "a very large percentage" is; 90, 80 per cent?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: In that realm, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If there was a plan to destroy all or a large and significant part of that population, the Serbs at that time were in a position to carry that out, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, I believe they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In fact, the reality is, is it not, that the large majority of the population were, in due course, either released or exchanged; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes. A lot were released; a lot were exchanged in return for prisoners of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And not killed as part of a plan to destroy,, in whole or in part, the Muslim population, were they?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Obviously, those that were released weren't killed, but there were many who weren't released who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If, on the other hand, there was a plan to kill all males of a reproductive age, again in large part, that group was either captive or under the control of the Serbian authorities, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: There was a large proportion of that population that were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And available for destruction if there was such a plan; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In fact, it's right, isn't it, that a large majority of those people forming that group were, after their detention in Batkovic, subsequently, as you've told us, released or exchanged; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Again, would you accept this proposition: If what was taking place in Brcko in May or June 1992 was a plan to destroy, in whole or in part, the Muslims, all those who were being released or exchanged would be potential witnesses to give evidence about that plan, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree with that proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I can't put myself inside their minds or know what their state of knowledge about what the Serb authorities proposed to do was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The report that you got from -- I'll remind myself of his name -- Mr. Avlijas points initially to one of those parts about Brcko, to an allegation of 2.500 being killed?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But, in fact, the extent of bodies in graves that we can point to, would you accept, is 226?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: The extent of bodies in graves that Mr. Avlijas refers to is 226. I'm unable to say that that is the full total or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That is the maximum number of bodies discovered which can be demonstrated as having potentially been killed in the relevant period, isn't it, Mr. Ralston?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Sorry. You said that the maximum -- could you repeat your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Two-hundred and twenty-six is the maximum number of bodies that have been discovered which can be demonstrated as having potentially been killed at the relevant period, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I don't know whether it is the maximum number of bodies that have been discovered. There are various organisations that are involved in recovering bodies. That's what's recovered in that report. I believe there's evidence of what we uncovered in an exhumation that the OTP conducted. There are various other people who are reported as missing who aren't detailed in these documents. So I can't say whether that's the maximum number of bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of those 226, some are reported as having died of natural causes; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let's assume for the moment that 226 is the extent of the killings at the relevant period. Would you accept that that would represent, of the Muslims of Brcko town, about 1 per cent of its 1991 population?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: There are a number of assumptions in there which -- firstly, I don't agree with your first assumption, so it's very difficult to follow on to the assumption that you're concluding with. If you're asking for a mathematical equation, is 226 1 per cent of however many thousand it is, my math isn't that good straightaway, but it may well be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you help us about this, please: You've used a word which can cover many things in describing the numbers of deaths overall in Bosnia-Herzegovina; the phrase you used was "thousands."

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you please be more specific as to what you claim you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Let the interpreter interpret the question, please; otherwise, it's very disturbing because I can't follow any -- at least as regards the French booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, we aren't getting the same messages that you are getting, so we don't know that someone is saying to you, "Please go more slowly." I'm not hearing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. It was not a criticism I was making of you. I was just thinking about my own comfort and, of course, the comfort of the interpreters. Please proceed. Would you ask your question again? Let me ask the French booth to do it again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can you remember the question, Mr. Ralston?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: If I go back, you're asking me how I arrive at the figure of thousands and can I be more specific. I think it's an unfortunate feature of this conflict that nobody has got a definite picture of how many people perished. There are claims, in relation to Muslim deaths, by Bosnian government officials of up to 200.000. I think there are currently in the vicinity of 20.000 people still reported as missing by the ICRC. In the course of statements we have taken, and we, by no means, have covered every municipality or every village in every municipality in Bosnia-Herzegovina or in Republika Srpska, but from the locations that we have dealt with, I think they're around 3.000 people who have been recorded as deceased.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I ask you this, please, would you accept this as a proposition: that if you wanted to persuade large numbers of people to either leave or to flee an area, that disseminating wide-spread knowledge of murders and beatings would act as a strong persuasive reason for people to leave?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: If it was disseminated in such a manner as the people believed the threat was real.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And would you agree with this: that by releasing large numbers of people who had either witnessed killings and so on or had heard from witnesses to such incidents, that is one effective way of making such knowledge wide-spread?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Paragraph 14, page 5, fourth paragraph down on that page, Mr. Ralston.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just as a general proposition, and this is not intended to suggest that killings and beatings are legitimate in any way, but would you accept that internment is a legitimate measure often taken by states in time of war?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think there are some very clear guidelines in the international law that deal with that proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, and that's why I didn't mean to suggest that the killings and so on were part of the legitimacy of that. Let me make that absolutely plain. Just answer the question: Is internment a legitimate measure often taken by states when faced with war?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I can't answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You were asked about the establishment of the facility at Luka. What you have in your report, as opposed to the phrase "around the 7th or 8th of May," the phrase you use in your report is "which was established on the 7th or 8th of May, 1992." Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just simply, as far as the final subparagraph of that paragraph 14 is concerned, and this is simply to make it clear, it is not accepted that any killings were solely on the basis of ethnicity, and so we disagree on that. Paragraph 15, Mr. Ralston, the second part of that paragraph, you refer to activities of the Serb forces and a pattern being established. It's right, isn't it, that similar operations were carried out in Bosnia by other warring parties; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I don't think the pattern was exactly the same, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The pattern may not have been exactly the same, but similar operations were conducted, for example, in the Konjic area, Bradina was occupied in a very similar sort of way and people expelled from it; do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can we turn now, please, to the documents? If you can go to tab number 1, and just as a general comment about the -- or general observation about the documents as a whole, the sort of documents that we see here, planning documents, have you seen similar documents that were prepared by other parties into the various conflicts that took place?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: No, I haven't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: As far as tab number 1 is concerned, looking at the top part of the document, it says this: "Because of the danger of the party's bureaucratisation and self-congratulatory isolation within a circle of the party's officials separated from the people, the President ... issues the following ..." Would you accept that that is sound, good advice for any political party wishing to remain in contact with its grass-root members?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think the wording is there for the Court to make its own decision on as to what that means.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you accept that that is what -- that the requirement in that document is for people to be in touch with those on the ground?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's the requirement, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: To stay in contact with 10 to 20 houses.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, further than that but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Of course, but that's one element of it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And it's expressed in that top paragraph as being the objective behind the document; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: No, I'm not clear on what you're getting at there. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Well, the stated purpose of the document is that which I read out, in other words, recognising the danger of the party becoming separated from the people, the instructions are issued because of that danger, and, therefore, the objective of the document as a whole is to ensure that people remain in touch with the grass roots. That's the effect of that, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think it could be interpreted in that way, or it could also be interpreted as being an awareness that if they don't keep in contact with the people and through the local boards, they may not necessarily be as attuned as to what's going on. But, to me, what that means is that they want to have communications with what's going on on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Tab 2, Mr. Ralston, the document of the 19th of December, 1991, would you look to page 2, please, paragraph 1, subparagraph 1? Does that speak of the tasks and so on set out in the instructions, "will be carried out within the national community of the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to implement the plebiscite decision whereby the Serb people in Bosnia and Herzegovina decided to live in a single state both in the existing conditions and circumstances and all those that may arise, bearing in mind the development of the entire political and security situation"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Firstly, can you help me about this: About two months before that, is it right that there had been a move in parliament by the SDA and the HDZ to pursue the issue of independence and sovereignty for Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You don't know. I see. It's plain at this stage, the Bosnian Serbs are aspiring to statehood. Would you accept that that's an influence which might properly be drawn from that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's an inference, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you accept that the sort of measures that are set out in these documents are measures which might typically be taken by an aspirant state?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say what an aspirant state would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: At tab 3, Mr. Ralston, please, Bijeljina, which is supposed to be one of the municipal centres, would you accept that that is an important town in its own right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, I would accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And it forms the centre of the Semberija region, which is the agricultural region at that northeastern corner of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's the area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Can I ask you now, please, about your report, paragraphs 22 and 23? Can you just remind me, how long have you been the chief investigator for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Since April 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Dealing with the killings and so on and the setting up of camps, again just in the interests of a degree of historical balance, the Serbs were not the only people who were setting up such camps or the only people who were engaging in killings, were they?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Indeed, one of the trials before this Tribunal has involved a camp set up by Muslim authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Paragraphs 25 and 26, please. You discuss there the targeting of Bosnian, Muslim, and Croat intellectuals, professional, political, and religious leaders. Have you undertaken any investigation at all into the degree to which other parties, other than the SDA, such as the SDP, the Reform Coalition, and the MBO, firstly had Muslim members and, secondly, the extent to which those Muslims were targeted, or not?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I haven't separated the people out from those parties. I'm aware that some from the MBO were targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Finally dealing, please, with the mass graves, you are reliant on essentially secondhand information in relation to those identifications that were made; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: If you're referring to identifications that were made as a result of investigation work that we've done, I'm relying on reports that have been prepared and presented to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No, I'm not referring to that. I'm referring to the identifications set out in the lists which are attached to the documents we've got.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes. Umm --

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Those are at secondhand, that information. Would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Certainly secondhand when it comes to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You cannot say and cannot demonstrate if the identifications which are made therein -- either how they came to be made or if they were accurate; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I can't say how they arrived at the material they put in there. Some of the work that our staff have done subsequent have confirmed some of those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You can't say on what date the documents, which are the lists, on what date those documents were created?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Or for what purpose they were created?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Or by whom they were created?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I would have to check the documents again, I think. My recollection in relation to these documents is that they were documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What document are you talking about, Mr. Greaves? Could you clarify? What document are you referring to; the lists which are in Exhibit 69, or are you referring to List 12 or, rather, Exhibit 12 or 13? What lists are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The lists which this witness has produced as part of his evidence. In other words, the lists that you first mentioned. I don't think this witness has given any evidence at all about Exhibit 12 whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite. That is why I wanted to be sure. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The lists which we have been talking about, Mr. Ralston, is it your understanding that where the date appears, for example, "6th of May", "9th of May", that purports to be the date on which deaths took place or something else?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's the date on the top of the document. Whether it's the date the deaths took place or whether it was the date they were recorded, I'm in no position to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Finally, Mr. Ralston, paragraph 33 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if we might just go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Could you please, Mr. Ralston, take your bundle of documents, and I'm going to ask you to put a finger in two different pages. For those reading in the French, it's towards the back of the bundle, about six pages, seven pages -- no, eight or nine pages in, and it's page 6294 in the top right-hand corner. For those following in English, and this can be put on the ELMO, it would be page 584614.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you please do that, usher. Thank you, thank you. I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: This is one of the pages, if you're looking at 4614 in the English, and also keeping an 6294 in the French, this is the translation of one of the pages of names provided to you by Avlijas in his report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If we -- and you've been asked questions about its reliability or unreliability and so on. If we look at, on 614, that's the English, the second name down, which is number 3, on the French if we look in about the middle of the page under the 9th of May, do we, in each case, find Hasan Jasarevic, son of Salih, born on the 10th of December, 1961, and is that a name in respect of which this defendant has, in fact, pleaded guilty?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to that. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It's a matter of record. If we go down further on the same pages to the number 13 on each case, Suad Hadzic, born on the 30th of September, 1956, again is that a name -- and again these are examples only -- in respect of which this defendant has pleaded guilty?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Again, I'm aware of the fact the defendant has pleaded guilty in relation to some people, but the names, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Very well. But staying in the same place on those two pages, if we go on two further names to number 15, do we see a male body, aged about 45, Ahmet Hodzic, also known as Papa?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: So whether or not you know of what happened to Papa or whether he was covered in the evidence, is this an example of these lists, by whomsoever they were compiled, using nicknames?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If you've looked at the list in detail recently, can you recall whether there may be other examples of nicknames used in the compilation of these lists?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes, there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You've been asked about the reliability of Avlijas' figure of 2.500, and you've been asked about issues of propaganda and so on, or the dissemination of information for purposes of moving populations and so on. At the time that this report was provided to you, can you think of any reason why Avlijas should overstate the number of people in the graves at Brcko?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: On that topic, mass graves, some five were opened in Brcko, and of those, one had plainly been robbed and one was either empty because it had been emptied or because it had never been used. But do you know if that was the totality of the suspected sites of mass graves at Brcko or if there were other suspected sites?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I don't believe that was the total of suspected sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Locating sites of mass graves in communities like this, notwithstanding the presence in the towns of people who must have been there at the relevant times, is it an easy task, a middling task, or a difficult task?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: It's a difficult task.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Even to identify?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Even to identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let's turn to questions that you were asked about the numbers who did not die and who survived. At the time of the stopping of the killings in Brcko, can you help us with what was the state of international awareness of what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Can you be more specific with the date range you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Yes. This is towards the 14th, 15th of May, 17th maybe.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: At that time, international awareness to the state of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina was raised to such an extent that various members of the UNPROFOR, which had commenced to set up its establishment in Sarajevo, withdrew to Bosnia, so -- withdrew to Belgrade. I think it's fair to say that at that stage, the International Community became far more aware about what was going on in the various areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: One other topic on this very issue that's been raised in evidence by a witness and upon which your comment might be helpful, in light of the questions that have been asked, was to the effect that there may at that time have been Serb prisoners who were themselves captive and were, if I can put it in this way, ripe for exchange, and that there was therefore a need for live prisoners to exchange. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I'm not sure that the need and the heightened awareness of having prisoners for exchange came about at the start of my or sometime after my -- when the situation of prisoner exchanges became, I think, somewhat more regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Forget, for the time being, Brcko, but focus simply on the rest of your evidence which dealt with the area generally. Was the stopping of killing by any side, not just the Serbs, was the stopping of killing ever associated with the need to have live prisoners for exchange, or is that simply someone's theory that we should discount?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I don't know -- I don't think it's a theory you can discount. I don't think it's a proven fact, either. What we are aware of anecdotally is that at particular stages, it became useful to have prisoners to exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. Questions were put to you about a part of a group being killed. They were, in a sense, perhaps, legal questions which will have to be addressed by the Chamber in due course. But arising from the questions that you were asked, just this: Notwithstanding the numbers that may have been released, of those who were killed, were there common denominators amongst those killed? Were there special selection criteria for those who were killed, in your experience?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: It appears to me that there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Namely?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: People in prominent positions, intellectuals, community leaders, people with higher education.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Then finally as a matter of detail, in the course of his questions of you about ethnic cleansing, Mr. Greaves used the word "evacuation", and you responded to it without querying its use. But just so that we can get our terminology right, is "evacuation" an appropriate synonym for "ethnic cleansing", in your judgement, or not? What word, if any, would you choose, if not "evacuation"?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: The words I would use would be "forcible transfer".

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That concludes my re-examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Judge Riad, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] Good afternoon, Mr. Ralston.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: On the procedure, you're helping me to see what lays through the thrust of your testimony without going into many details. You mentioned, almost at the outset, that on the 3rd of May, the paramilitary and the JNA and others ethnically cleansed their own Serbs from certain areas, which brings us to the issue of cleansing. You mentioned that killing was not an uncommon procedure in cleansing. I'm rather familiar with the other English statement. Would that mean that killing was a normal method of cleansing?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was. It was a normal method of cleansing.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Then coming to the question of the Prosecutor, when he mentioned the deportation or forced transfer, which of these methods were used more commonly?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Forced transfer where people were forced across what became the confrontation line to the other side of the territory, then in subsequent times, when the International Community became more aware, people were then transferred into other countries and not internally into Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So priority was given to deportation or to killing, or was it a question of time, that it changed according to the world public opinion.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: It changed according to time and world public opinion. In the events at the start of May, the first characterisation of it was rounding up people in the villages. People who were killed during that process, they were incarcerated, and then it got into the process of what they were going to do with the people who were incarcerated. Some were beaten, some were tortured, some were killed, and some were released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, as far as killing is concerned, you mentioned that any Muslim was targeted and that thousands were subjected to killings. Was it completely indiscriminate? Was it a completely indiscriminate process, regardless of whether they were old, young, women, children?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I don't think it was completely indiscriminate. We have evidence of people being called out on the basis of lists, which indicates to me that there was some selectivity about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Which brings me to the other question of the Prosecutor, because now I want to reconcile the idea that you mentioned that any Muslim was a target, and then there was a selection. You mentioned that the selection would be the elite. So was it some kind of extermination of the elite to start with?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think both things happened. There were people who were killed purely on the basis that they were Muslim. We also have material which indicates that if you are from one of the groups that I mentioned, you're more likely to have been called out and killed or beaten or ill-treated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Sorry. Would you just repeat to me the groups you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Intelligentsia, intellectuals, people with higher education, prominent people, professional people, community leaders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was there any percentage for this extermination, or was it open, whether in quantity or quality?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think it was more in quality than quantity, but it's difficult for me to give you a percentage because the numbers are different in the different areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: For instance, they wouldn't say, "We would like to get rid of 50 per cent of the population," that sort of thing, or was it an open process?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think it was an open process. I'm not aware of anyone who said that they wanted to get rid of "X" per cent of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And the intelligentsia and the elite first?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Now, just in passing, a question which I didn't understand. You say some people were released and then captured again.

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What was the idea behind it?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I'm not sure why they were released, but I think it's a matter of record that some of those who were released were then subsequently detained again and transferred -- once they were detained, taken to the Batkovic camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was it for reasons of exchange, for instance, to prove that -- so that the others from the other side, from the opposite side, could be released?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Rodrigues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Ralston. I have several questions regarding the lists. In order to make our dialogue easier, I am following Exhibit 69/6. Here, we have a translation of a document and we have noticed here 616 persons in total, and then we have -- 63 have been identified, 8 died of natural causes, 9 were women. But if I know my arithmetic, then it comes up to 120. Is there perhaps a mistake in the document, or does this figure mean something else?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think that tally does not include the number of bodies that were unidentified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So in one of the same documents, a distinction is made before the 10th of July -- let me try to put it clearer. Between the 1st of July -- no, excuse me. There is a distinction between the 1st of May, 1992 and the 10th of July. After the 10th of July, the document says that persons -- that killed persons were buried in a cemetery with a religious ceremony and that their burial was indicated and that the site is known. Could one conclude that before the 10th of July, people were not buried with a proper religious service, in a cemetery, and that their graves were not indicated in any way? Is that what it means?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think it could mean that. I think, from the evidence that we have, the people that are contained in the lists weren't buried in a cemetery or marked with -- in marked graves or with religious rites. Certainly, when we conduct an exhumation at these grave sites, they are sites which were actually covered in tons and tons of rubble. And none of the steps report about marking the graves or that religious rites had actually been carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question, Mr. Ralston. Could these dates, those differences indicated by dates, could that allow us to conclude that before the 10th of July, there was an intent to hide the bodies?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think that's an inference you could draw, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Then I'm moving to another list, at least I'm still in binder 6 and I'm referring to the list which is of the 5th/6th May. The first 16 persons on the list are identified, or have been identified, and the rest of them, that is, down to the 33rd, have not been identified. Do you believe there is a reason behind the identification of the first 16 persons, and then a complete lack of identification for the rest of them? Do you think there is a reason behind it? Excuse me. I want to ask you another question. Is there a relationship between the identification of persons and non-identification of persons?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: There may well be, but I don't know what the relationship is or the reason why some are identified and some aren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question, Mr. Ralston. There is yet another list, the list with about 160 persons, and for some of them, it says that they died of natural causes. The other names on the list alongside those names where it is not indicated that they died of natural causes, does that mean that they met a violent death?

utterances.speaker: PAUL ANTHONY BASHAM
utterances.text: I think that's the conclusion I'd draw, if it was -- if it's not of natural causes, that it would be a violent death, yes. Whether it -- yes. That's difficult to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Ralston.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Ralston. I do not have any particular questions to ask you. The Tribunal wishes to thank you for placing at our disposal your knowledge and your appreciation of the situation. Now we shall make a break, but before that -- don't move, Mr. Ralston -- I should like to hear from Mr. Nice. What are you envisaging after Mr. Ralston's testimony? Have you now completed your case or do you have any more witnesses to call?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Subject to one point I want to raise about witnesses, which I should do in private session, yes, we've completed our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I have to confer with my colleagues for a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Judges are ready to make another small effort, and I hope the interpreters will not mind to hear that, but first we shall have to escort Mr. Ralston, unless you need Mr. Ralston's presence here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, thank you. I'm happy for him to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Lordships.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are now in private session.
